The Large woodshrike Tephrodornis virgatus is a passerine inhabiting broadleaved forests across Southeast Asia, where its life-history traits reflect adaptation to a relatively stable tropical environment. Field studies have documented that freshly laid eggs average 21.6 mm in length and 15.7 mm in width, yielding an initial wet weight of approximately 2.8 grams [Ww0 = approximately 2.8 grams] based on the standard formula for an ellipsoid. The incubation period unfolds at a mean nest temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C], under which the eggs hatch after 12 days [ab = 12 days]. This relatively brief incubation is consistent with patterns observed in other malaconotoid species of comparable size. The nestlings grow rapidly and are capable of sustained flight by 13 days after hatching [tx = 13 days after hatching], a developmental pace that is accelerated compared to many temperate zone passerines, likely an adaptation that reduces the window of vulnerability to nest predation in dense tropical forests at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C].

Reproductive rates in Tephrodornis virgatus have been quantified in several long term population studies, with particular attention to the physiological conditions experienced by breeding adults. At an ambient temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], which corresponds to the thermal conditions during the core of the breeding season in the lowland portions of its range, females reach puberty 39 days after hatching [tp = 39 days after hatching]. This rapid maturation allows individuals to attempt breeding relatively early in their first year. The interval between hatching and the initiation of the first brood is 1.1 years since birth [tR = 1.1 years since birth], a timing that reflects the interplay between gonadal development and the seasonal availability of arthropod prey at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. The maximum recorded lifespan under natural conditions at this same thermal regime is approximately 6.25 years [am = approximately 6.25 years], though most individuals likely experience higher mortality rates during the post fledging dispersal phase at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C].

Adult females of the Large woodshrike attain an ultimate wet weight of 39 grams [Wwi = 39 grams], representing the asymptotic body mass reached once somatic growth is complete. This body size places them among the smaller members of the Vangidae family, and it corresponds to a predictable metabolic demand. Resting metabolic rate measurements obtained via flow through respirometry at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C] yielded a basal oxygen consumption of 88.38 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 88.38 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This value is consistent with allometric predictions for a passerine of this mass, though it sits at the upper end of the confidence interval, possibly reflecting the elevated thermoregulatory costs associated with maintaining activity in a persistently warm environment. The developmental schedule of the Large woodshrike integrates these physiological capacities with the seasonal phenology of its habitat. Hatchlings emerge from eggs incubated at the stable temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C], a thermal regime that ensures consistent embryo development. The age at hatching is 12 days [ab = 12 days], after which the altricial nestlings depend entirely on biparental provisioning at a temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C]. By 13 days after hatching [tx = 13 days after hatching], the young are capable of their first flight, an early fledging age that shortens the period of maximal nest vulnerability at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. Sexual maturation, defined by the onset of gonadal activity, is attained at 39 days after hatching [tp = 39 days after hatching], a rapid transition that allows birds hatched early in the season to breed before the end of the same reproductive period at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This accelerated life history is notable given the moderate adult body mass and the relatively high metabolic rate the species sustains.

At the population level, the annual reproductive output of Tephrodornis virgatus is primarily constrained by clutch frequency rather than clutch size. Under the thermal regime of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], females achieve a maximum of 2.8 clutches per year [F_R_i = 2.8 clutches per year] and produce approximately 1 egg per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 1 egg per clutch]. The time from hatching to the first successful brood is 1.1 years since birth [tR = 1.1 years since birth], indicating that most individuals delay their first breeding attempt until the second breeding season after they hatch at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. These demographic parameters, considered together with the rapid juvenile development and early sexual maturation, suggest a life history strategy that balances high early mortality risk against the potential for repeated breeding attempts across several seasons.
